questions.title: technology
questions.passage: Have you ever wondered how a phone knows which way you are facing? Inside almost every modern smartphone sits a tiny device called a magnetometer. questions.title: artificial light and sleep
questions.passage: Many people stay awake long after sunset because their homes are full of bright artificial light. Small changes to our evening light may protect the rest we badly need.

questions.title: the history of paper
questions.passage: Long before printers and notebooks, people struggled to find good surfaces for writing. In ancient times, some carved letters into stone, while others pressed marks into wet clay or wrote on dried animal skins. These materials were heavy, costly, or hard to prepare, so written records stayed rare. Then, many centuries ago in China, people learned to make a light material by soaking plant fibers in water and pressing them into thin sheets. Once the sheets dried, they became smooth and easy to write on, and this invention slowly spread to other lands. Traders and travelers carried the knowledge along busy routes, and new workshops appeared in distant cities. Because this new material was cheaper than skins, more people could keep notes, write letters, and share ideas. Schools and libraries grew as books became easier to copy and store. The simple sheet you write on today is the result of that long, patient history. It quietly changed how humans remember and pass on what they know.

questions.title: memory and learning
questions.passage: When you try to remember something new, your brain does far more than simply store a picture of it. It links the new fact to things you already know, building a web of connections that makes the memory easier to find later. Testing yourself, rather than just reading the same page again, forces your mind to pull the information out, and that effort helps it stick. The more thoughtfully you practice, the more reliably you will recall what you learn.

questions.title: folk tales
questions.passage: In a village ringed by tall hills, there once lived a weaver named Soraya who was known for her patience. As the blanket grew, so did the laughter, and the villagers shared stories until the long night passed. By morning the worst of the cold had broken. questions.title: space
questions.passage: Not every planet circles a star. Astronomers have gradually realized that the galaxy holds an enormous number of so-called rogue worlds, planets that drift through space without orbiting any sun at all. Some were probably born around a star and later flung outward when a larger neighbor disturbed their path. Others may have formed alone, condensing directly from cold clumps of gas and dust. Because these wanderers give off almost no light of their own, they are extraordinarily difficult to detect. Researchers usually find them indirectly, watching for the brief moment when a rogue planet passes in front of a distant star and bends its light like a lens. Conditions on such worlds sound bleak, since their surfaces receive no warmth from a nearby sun. Yet scientists point out that a thick atmosphere, or heat leaking from a planet's core, might keep some regions surprisingly mild. A few even speculate that a hidden ocean could survive beneath a frozen crust. For now, these lonely planets remind us how much of the universe still lies beyond our easy view.

questions.title: the brain

It unfolds quietly, connection by connection, long after a lesson appears finished.
